idea-plugin.name: Deju Trace
idea-plugin.description:
Deju Trace follows a single targeted live API call through a running Java web app and paints the executed source line/branch coverage back into the editor like JUnit coverage, but for one real request.
  • Green: line fully executed
  • Yellow: decision point where only some branches were taken
  • Red: a line inside an entered method that never executed
Place a "deju point" on a controller/entry method, hit the endpoint, and see the code traces. Keeps the last 5 executions and exports a self-contained HTML report: a call tree in exact execution order, syntax-highlighted source, and the SQL each line issued. Entities, DTOs and generated builders can be folded out of it, so the report shows the code you are actually debugging.

Works against a JVM you launch from the IDE, one in a Docker container, or one on another machine.

The companion agent is attached by you via -javaagent. It listens on loopback only by default; reaching it from a container or another host takes an explicit bind=, and the agent refuses to start on any non-loopback address unless a token is set. The plugin generates that token for you when it writes the VM option. No variable values are captured. SQL statement text is recorded so queries appear in the call tree, but bound parameters are never read and stay as ? placeholders. There is no telemetry.

What Deju records… in Settings shows every file the plugin has written, what each one holds, and what is never captured. Clear Deju data… removes all of it, and uninstalling from a running IDE does the same.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
2.0.2: the agent ships as its own release asset

  • Fixed: the standalone agent jar was never built. Every release now produces deju-agent-<version>.jar alongside the plugin zip. The task that makes it existed but was wired to nothing, so it only ran if you invoked it by name, and the versioned asset was missing from the release.
  • This is what a containerised JVM downloads. A setup script pins DEJU_VERSION and fetches that file, so the agent in the container always matches the plugin in the IDE; without the version in the name, a cached copy survives a bump and surfaces much later as a protocol mismatch. The copy bundled in the plugin keeps its fixed deju-agent.jar name and is byte-identical to the published one.

2.0.1: three ways to read one request

  • The report is now three tabs. Code Trace is everything the report already did, unchanged. Graph and Flow Chart are new, and neither is built until you open it, so the file still opens instantly and a reader who only wants the trace pays nothing for the rest.
  • Graph ranks files by the time they actually cost, their own code plus the SQL they issued, each query charged to the method that issued it. Self time on its own hides the database entirely, and totals double-count every caller up the stack, so neither answers "which file is slow" by itself. Include SQL switches between the two readings.
  • N+1 detection. A file that issues the same statement more than once carries a ×N badge with the statement and its total cost, and the run's worst offender is named at the top of the tab. Matching ignores whitespace and case, so the same query built two ways still groups.
  • Flow Chart draws the call tree on a canvas, top to bottom in execution order. Click a step to fold its calls away; a run of identical sibling calls collapses into one box marked ×5, which is usually what an N+1 looks like from the side. Queries are laid out on their clause lines in the box itself rather than trimmed to a hover.
  • Flame layout. Switch the diagram from nesting to time: box width is duration, with a time ruler across the top, click-to-zoom into any frame and a breadcrumb back out. Zoom stretches the time axis and not the text, so zooming out to compare shapes keeps the labels readable. Save PNG exports it.
  • Frames are coloured by owning class from a fixed palette checked for colour-blind separation against both themes, so two classes never share a hue and the narrow slivers stay tellable apart. Queries keep the SQL orange throughout.
  • Chrome moved out of the toolbar. Theme and help are icon buttons in the top-right corner, the code filter sits in the stats row at full height, and the "showing N of M" count now rides with the trace point.
  • Internal: replaced the deprecated platform comment component, so the plugin now reports zero deprecated API usages on 2024.1 through 2024.3.

1.3.0: reading the tree without the noise

  • Filter calls by time, three ways. The call filter offered only "at least this long". It now also does less than and between, with presets for each, and Custom… lets you pick the comparison and type the bounds (750us, 1.5 ms, 2s). Between-ranges are half-open, so the presets tile without a call landing in two of them.
  • Hide SQL, or the excluded-call summaries. Two toolbar toggles for reading control flow on its own: SQL hides every query and folded query run, Excluded rows hides the "… N excluded calls" summaries.
  • Long queries are trimmed to three lines with Show full query to open them, so a trace with thirty statements is still a call tree rather than a wall of SQL.
  • Show opens 5 files rather than 10. Every recorded file is still painted, so opening one by hand shows its coverage immediately; the limit only governs how many tabs appear unasked. Configurable as before.
  • Total time reads in the unit you think in. It was always milliseconds, so a slow request showed "94812 ms". It now carries the larger unit alongside once it reaches one: 94812 ms (1m 34s).
  • Step numbers are numbered badges instead of "#1", and the report header carries a Code Traces chip.
  • Fixed: the Files view hid the top of every method section. A stray overflow on the file card made it the nearest scroll container, which stopped the sticky file header positioning against the page and left it sitting on top of the method heading below it.
  • Fixed: the custom time-filter field appeared on load instead of waiting for Custom… to be chosen.

1.2.0: SQL in the trace, and a report you can actually read

  • Docker without a port-forwarding sidecar. The agent takes a new bind= argument, so a containerised JVM can expose its control socket the same way the JVM's own debugger does: bind=0.0.0.0 plus a published port, and the IDE connects straight to it. The default is still loopback-only, and the agent refuses to listen on any other address unless a token is set. Tick Traced JVM runs in a container or on another machine in Settings and Copy agent VM option fills the argument in for you.
  • SQL queries appear in the call tree, at the line that issued them, with their own timing. Statement text only; bound parameters are never read and stay as ? placeholders, and nothing is captured unless a trace is armed. Statements are formatted onto clause lines and syntax-coloured, long ones are trimmed to three lines with an expand control, and a toolbar toggle hides SQL entirely for reading control flow on its own.
  • Java syntax highlighting in the exported report, in both light and dark themes (keywords, strings, comments, annotations and types), instead of the flat monochrome the report used to show.
  • The report has been redesigned around the platform's own look: system typography, a monospace face that matches the IDE editor, hairline borders, a translucent toolbar that stays put while you scroll, and a segmented control in place of the old buttons. Light and dark are both first-class.
  • Smaller reports. The embedded logo was a 1024×1024 image shown at 28 pixels and carried twice, costing ~149 KB in every file; it is now sized for the job. Export also offers an Essential mode that leaves excluded types' source out of the document rather than shipping it and hiding it.
  • The Files picker now works in the Tree view too, so a trace can be stripped down to one layer, and long class names are no longer truncated.
  • Excluded types. A single request touches dozens of entities, DTOs and generated builders that are not what you are debugging. The report's new Essential view folds them into one "… N excluded calls" row at the call site, keeping the count and total time visible; Full still shows every recorded frame. A call is only folded when everything underneath it is also excluded, so a getter that triggers a lazy load stays on screen with the query it caused.
  • Choose the types under Settings → Tools → Deju Trace: case-insensitive globs by class name (*dto, *entity) or by package (*.dto.*), plus your own. Per-class exclusions… overrides any pattern for one class, in either direction. Nested classes follow their outer class, so excluding a response wrapper also excludes the builder generated inside it. Stored per project; the recording itself is never filtered.
  • Show opens 5 files instead of all of them, in execution order, the traced method's own file first. Every recorded file is still painted, so opening one of the others later shows its coverage and timings immediately. The limit is configurable (0 = no limit) and what was not opened is named in a notification.
  • Run configurations repair themselves. A -javaagent path pinned to a previous build stops the JVM from starting at all once the plugin updates. Fix run configurations rewrites the path in place, preserving your port/token/includes arguments and leaving any non-Deju agent untouched; Refresh agent on disk re-extracts the bundled jar.
  • The plugin now reports which agent build is actually loaded in the traced JVM and warns when it is older than the installed plugin, the usual cause of a report missing newer features, since a -javaagent is fixed at process start and needs the application restarted.
  • You can see, and delete, everything Deju keeps. What Deju records… in Settings lists every file the plugin has written, what is in it, its size, and what is never captured, with a button to open each location. Clear Deju data… removes the lot: recorded runs, exclusion rules, connection settings and the extracted agent, naming anything it could not delete rather than reporting success. Uninstalling from the Plugins page of a running IDE clears the same data.
  • The connection token is generated per installation. It used to ship as a fixed string in the plugin source, which is not a secret, and it is the only thing guarding the agent socket once bind= opens it beyond loopback.
  • Recorded runs no longer risk reaching a commit. They live under .idea/ and contain executed SQL statement text, so the directory now carries its own .gitignore instead of relying on yours.
  • Fixed: Copy agent VM option handed out a path that broke on the next update. It named the version-stamped jar, which is renamed and deleted whenever the plugin updates, so a flag pasted into a compose file, a Gradle build or an env var would fail at JVM start with "Error opening zip file or JAR manifest missing". It now gives the fixed-name path, which stays valid across updates.
  • Fixed: the tool window forced a horizontal scrollbar when docked at its usual width. Its controls wrapped onto new rows but still reported their width as if they were on one line, so the panel always claimed to be wider than the dock.

1.1.0: the HTML report becomes a call tree

  • New default view: Tree. Every method invocation in exact execution order, each numbered with the step it ran at, with each method's own lines interleaved with the calls it made, placed at the line that made them. A trace now reads top to bottom.
  • Per-call inclusive timing, a hot path highlight that follows the slowest chain, and a minimum-time filter. Neither ever reorders the tree.
  • Runs of identical sibling calls fold automatically, so an N+1 query loop no longer floods the page. Click to expand; order is preserved.
  • Files view: lines are grouped into named method sections; file headers stick to the top and carry line, unexecuted and timing counts; long reports open collapsed so they read as an index.
  • Click any line number to open it in the IDE (requires JetBrains Toolbox), with Copy path as a fallback.
  • Keyboard navigation throughout; press ? for the full list.
  • Fixed: "API order" sorted by hash-set iteration order instead of the order classes were actually entered, making it effectively arbitrary.
  • Fixed: "Slowest first" ranked by inclusive time, which always favoured whatever sat highest on the call stack. Self time and total time are now separate options: self time finds the method actually doing the slow work.
  • Unchanged guarantees: no variable capture, no telemetry, and no network calls or remote resources in the exported report.

0.1.0: initial MVP, line/branch coverage for one targeted call, last-5 history, and HTML export.
